title: Living ashtpadi 18
hook: the bond of Guru and Sikh runs both ways

segments.voice: Yesterday, nihkaamee: serving without wanting anything back, and finding yourself filled. Today we close the eighteenth ashtpadi with a famous day in 1699.

Anandpur, at the spring festival of Vaisakhi, 1699, as Sikh tradition tells it. A huge crowd. Guru Gobind Singh stands before them with a drawn sword and asks for a head. Silence. Then one man stands up. Then another, and another, until five have come forward. The Guru initiates them with amrit, sweetened water stirred with a double-edged sword, and names them the Panj Pyare, the five beloved ones. Everyone expects that to be the climax. It isn't. What the Guru does next is the part Sikhs still sing about.
screen: `VAISAKHI, 1699.` → `FIVE COME FORWARD.` → `WHAT THE GURU DOES NEXT.`

segments.voice: Having initiated the five, the Guru kneels before them and asks them to initiate him in the same way. The teacher takes amrit from his own students. A later poet, writing in the tradition of Bhai Gurdas, put it in a line Sikhs still sing: wonderful is Gobind Singh, himself the Guru and himself the disciple. Aape gur chela. That moment is the eighteenth ashtpadi, lived out. This week the ashtpadi showed two directions. The Guru toward the Sikh: cherishing, cleaning, freeing, holding the Sikh close, like his own life. The Sikh toward the Guru: living in the Guru's house, serving without wanting, making no show. Read separately, those could sound like a ladder, the Guru on top giving, the Sikh below serving. At Anandpur the ladder becomes a circle. The Guru serves the Sikhs; the Sikhs become a kind of Guru; the Khalsa, the community, is later called the Guru Panth. Care goes down, service goes up, and then they trade places. That's what both ways means. It's also why Sikhs describe the relationship as a bond rather than fear. In that telling, a Sikh keeps the daily banis, the five articles of faith, the honest work, not as payment to a distant master but as one half of a bond whose other half is already given. The Guru keeps faith with the Sikh. The Sikh keeps faith with the Guru. Neither half works alone. And on an ordinary day, that bond lives in very small things: one hymn read, one practice kept, one promise to the Guru not quietly dropped.
screen: `THE GURU KNEELS TO THE FIVE.` · `AAPE GUR CHELA.` · `A LADDER BECOMES A CIRCLE.` · `TWO HALVES OF ONE BOND.` · then, large: `BOTH WAYS.`

segments.voice: Choose one small practice to keep for the Guru, or for whatever teacher or path you're walking: these few minutes each day, one line of a hymn each morning, a single act of honest work done carefully. Then rest in the other half of the bond, the care others have already given you, noticed or not, and hold both halves together.
Panj Pyare, the five beloved ones Guru Gobind Singh initiated at Anandpur, who then initiated him in turn: Aape gur chela, himself Guru and disciple, care and service running both ways.
Your line: both ways. A practice kept is your half of a bond, not a payment. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 509 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ASHTPADI 19, SALOK: NOTHING GOES ALONG.`

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Vaisakhi 1699, when Guru Gobind Singh initiated the Panj Pyare and then received amrit from them, and sing the line aape gur chela; the eighteenth ashtpadi of Sukhmani describes the Guru's care and the Sikh's service.

original.note: Gurmukhi: chela, disciple, as in aape gur chela, himself Guru and disciple.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Guru leads and the Sikh follows. end of story.
what it means: the bond runs both ways; at Anandpur the Guru became disciple to his disciples.
what a scholar hears: the line vaah vaah Gobind Singh aape gur chela is attributed to Bhai Gurdas II (Vaar 41), and 1699 is remembered as the founding of the Khalsa.

chat.says: After Guru Gobind Singh initiated the first five, what did he do next?
options: Tradition says he knelt and asked the five to initiate him: himself Guru and disciple.
He sent the five away to teach, and never took amrit himself, since he was the Guru.
He chose five more people, and kept going until a hundred had come forward that day.
chat.meaning: Sikh tradition says Guru Gobind Singh took amrit from the Panj Pyare. A later poet sang: aape gur chela, himself the Guru and himself the disciple.
